newsitem.title: UK: Giant bags to tap islands' demand for fresh water.
newsitem.headline: Giant bags to tap islands' demand for fresh water.

text.p: A British company has found a fresh way to slake the growing thirst of dry Greek islands - by tugging thousands of tonnes of fresh water to them across the sea in giant floating bags.

London-based Aquarius Water Trading and Transportation Co is due to deliver its first fresh water this week from the Greek port of Piraeus to a nearby island after a local authority signed a contract to carry 290,000 tonnes from May to December.
"One bag is already in the water and is loading," said Gian Piero D'Amico, a director of Aquarius.
Looking like dark, shiny whales, each bag is made of strong woven polyester fabric, is 60 metres (almost 200 feet) long and can contain 700 tonnes of water in its woven fabric shell.

The patented bags are just two metres (six feet) deep, less than the draught of the conventional tankers, and small tugs can haul four or five full bags at once and drop them off one at time at different places, returning later to collect the empties.
"The old tankers they are using at the moment deliver water at a transport cost of $2.50 per tonne and our system is better than that," said Simon Pratt, Aquarius' managing director.
"We think we can bring the price down by 40 percent."
Per Gunnar Rymer, an analyst for Oslo-based brokerage Karl Johan Fonds, a subsidiary of the Union Bank of Norway, said over-the-counter shares in Aquarius were currently undervalued at $9 each.
"It is a new company which needs to establish a track record and we did not want to overshoot, so we made a conservative estimate of $20 per share," he said.
The floating populations of some Greek islands can quadruple in summertime as European tourists flood to their sun-spangled shores, and demand for water skyrockets.
Aquarius is currently targetting a handful of small islands near Piraeus and the first water will go from there to a nearby town called Kipseli, on the island of Aegina.

Kipseli has not previously imported water but is turning to Aquarius because local boreholes are becoming salty and are drying up - a problem on a number of Greek islands. It is also the current delivery point for 700,000 tonnes per year of water imports for Aegina town itself.
Aquarius is only responsible for transporting the water, while the local authorities pay the cost of the water itself.
"We are talking to a number of other local councils and they are all interested," said D'Amico.

A joint venture with a local tug company has helped bypass a number of bureaucratic obstacles, Pratt said, but added that deliveries this week were being conducted on a non-comercial basis because they were still waiting for a certificate from the Hellenic Merchant ships' inspectorate.

D'Amico said the initial contract at $1.20 per tonne would be loss-making but he hoped to sign contracts for up to 800,000 tonnes per year by the end of this year, and to reach a total of two million tonnes by the end of 1998.

Two other companies planning to use water bag technology - Spragg in California and Nordic Water Supply in Norway - are currently developing larger bags for different markets but they are both some way away from entering the market, he said.
"The market for water worldwide is really going to take off in the years to come," Rymer said.
Aquarius has already had signs of interest from as far as field as Spain and even Fiji.
"But we have to get Greece up and running first," Pratt said.
Investment so far in the project adds up to around $2 million - this includes the cost of building three finished prototype bags at around $100,000 each, as well as sea trials and marketing.
The company expects to be listed on the Small and Medium sized Business (SMB) list in Oslo next year and a fresh private placement of an additional 200,000 shares at $9 each is planned for next week.
"We believe there will be quite a lot of interest," Rymer said. "I have a feeling that water might be the next hot commodity."
